description: Team CSRG (胡居士說前世宇宙) is a four-member team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We work on the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge, combining web development, Python data processing, and astronomy. Our project includes an interactive viewer for infrared observations, data-processing tools, scientific analysis, a Jupyter notebook, and a research report. We are interested in making real astronomical data easier to explore, compare, and understand.
summary:
We developed a web-based viewer for comparing time-separated near-infrared observations of the same sky region from NASA’s SPHEREx mission. For the five challenge targets (Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis), Level 2 images from Data Release 1 and Quick Release 3, obtained from NASA/IPAC IRSA, were processed into 325 image products from 119 dated visits across all six detectors.

It addresses the challenge by enabling users to blink, play back and compare observations to search for moving and variable sources. Each frame reports its observation time, detector and wavelength, links to its original FITS file and can display the archive quality masks. Observations of asteroid Vesta demonstrate genuine motion, and a hypothetical Planet X model illustrates how a distant body would shift between visits. A research page provides a methods report, quality-aware photometry with uncertainties and an executable Jupyter notebook.

This work is important because SPHEREx observes each source at different wavelengths on different dates, so an apparent change may be instrumental rather than astrophysical. By making these effects explicit and keeping every result traceable to archive data, it enables students, citizen scientists and researchers to examine SPHEREx data reliably without specialized software.
details:
What it does and how it works

The project is a web-based viewer for comparing near-infrared observations of the same sky region taken by NASA's SPHEREx mission on different dates. A Python pipeline queries the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) for SPHEREx Level 2 spectral images that contain a given target and retrieves image cutouts. It reads the image, quality-flag, variance and spectral-coordinate extensions, and resamples each exposure onto a common 10-arcminute, north-up grid. From these exposures it builds dated visits, survey-pass stacks, difference images, shift-and-add images and colour composites. Every product is accompanied by a quality mask and a manifest that records its release, observation time, detector, wavelength and original FITS source.

For the five challenge targets (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis), the pipeline produced 325 products from 119 visits in Data Release 1 and Quick Release 3. In the browser, users can blink between images, play a sequence, step along a timeline, compare two images side by side or with a wipe, display masked pixels, inspect pixel coordinates, add notes, share links and export evidence as JSON. Observations of asteroid Vesta show genuine motion with its predicted positions overlaid. A hypothetical Planet X model uses the observatory's actual positions to show how a distant body would shift between visits. A research page provides a methods report, quality-aware aperture photometry with uncertainties, and an executable Jupyter notebook. An optional local service extends the same processing to any sky position.

Benefits and intended impact

The viewer makes SPHEREx time-domain data accessible without specialized software or programming. Because SPHEREx observes each source at different wavelengths on different dates, an apparent change can be instrumental rather than astrophysical. The viewer displays wavelength, detector and quality information next to every image, so users learn to separate real motion and variability from artifacts. We intend the tool to support students, educators and citizen scientists in searching for moving and variable objects, and to give researchers a quick, traceable way to inspect a field before working with the original FITS files.

Tools and technologies

  • Python 3.12 with Astropy and NumPy for archive access, FITS and WCS processing, and photometry, plus Flask for the optional live service.
  • TypeScript, HTML, CSS and Vite for the static web application, with HTML Canvas rendering and Aladin Lite for the sky context map.
  • Jupyter and Matplotlib for the reproducible analysis, and LaTeX for the report.
  • Docker, GitHub Actions, automated unit tests and headless Chrome browser tests.
  • Data: SPHEREx from IRSA, with Gaia DR3, 2MASS, AllWISE, JPL Horizons and CDS services for comparison, overlays and name resolution.

No special hardware was required. The site runs in any modern browser on desktop or mobile.

Creativity

The project adapts the classic blink comparison, used historically to discover Pluto and today in citizen-science searches, to a spectral survey whose wavelength changes between visits. It treats this time–wavelength confounding as a central part of the interpretation rather than hiding it. The Planet X model turns orbital parallax into an interactive demonstration, and every image and result remains traceable to its archive source.

Factors the team considered

  • Scientific validity: quality flags, saturation, masking and uncertainties are shown explicitly, and no detection or calibrated flux is claimed beyond what the data support.
  • Reproducibility: data products carry checksums and provenance, and the notebook's inputs are fixed.
  • Accessibility: the viewer needs no installation, supports English and Traditional Chinese, and works with mobile layouts and keyboard controls.
  • Cost and sustainability: the site is static and needs no server, and new SPHEREx releases can be added through configuration.
  • Data volume: each field uses a representative subset of exposures to keep the browser responsive.
  • Attribution: data, image and software credits are listed for every source used.
